passage1.text: Even though we are living in an age where growing old is thought of as an inevitable misery, this doctor has been changing the game for seniors over the last 25 years. It all started in 1991 when the Harvard-educated physician was transferred from working in a stressful emergency room to being the medical director of a nursing home in upstate New York. The depressing and regimented (严格管制的) environment got him thinking on what exactly could improve the residents' conditions. Even though animals in nursing homes were illegal at the time, Dr. Bill Thomas took a chance. Based on a hunch (直觉), he brought in two dogs, four cats, hens, rabbits, 100 birds, a multitude of plants, a flower garden, and a vegetable patch. The change was dramatic. There was a 50% drop in medical prescriptions along with a dramatic decrease in death rates—but most importantly, the residents were simply happier. Dr. Thomas's approach, named the Eden Alternative, has driven nursing homes to allow a more autonomous （自主的) and creative living space for their elderly. It erases the belief that growing old means growing useless. He encourages residents to think of their age as an enriching new phase of life rather than the end of it. Thomas, now a speaker and author of several books, also created small, independently-run residences with their own bedrooms and bathrooms, and he has been preaching a singular message that getting old is not a bad thing. "Within six weeks, they had to send a truck around to pick up all the wheelchairs," Thomas told the Washington Post. "You know why most people in nursing homes use wheelchairs? Because the buildings are so big." The 56-year-old doctor's methods have been adopted in Australia, Japan, Canada, and America with enormous success. Last year he published Second Wind: Navigating the Passage to a Slower, Deeper, and More Connected Life, a guide on how to shift our perspectives on aging and growth. He is currently traveling through North America performing with his guitar and his enthusiasm on his Age of Disruption Tour.

passage2.text: Research shows that in developed countries, more affluent and educated people tend to consume higher-quality diets-including more fruits and vegetables, fish and whole grains. On the contrary, economically disadvantaged people report diets that are nutrient-poor and energy-dense. They are less likely to have food-purchasing habits that conform to public health recommendations. These dietary differences are often accompanied by higher rates of obesity and diabetes among lower-income people. This relationship between social class and diet quality and health is extensively documented. However, the research does not explain why this is the case—a question that has significant implications for designing effective policies and initiatives to improve diets and prevent chronic diseases. Public-health initiatives to promote healthy diets often focus on providing nutrition education and recipes (食谱). These approaches, however, often presume less food literacy (i.e. food knowledge and skills) among low-income people. Are unhealthy diets really the result of poor choices, limited food skills and knowledge? Research suggests that adults in food-insecure households are just as likely as those in food-secure households to adjust recipes to make them more healthy. They are also just as proficient in food preparation and cooking skills. There is no indication that increasing food skills or budgeting skills will reduce food insecurity. Instead, disadvantaged groups are constrained by their economic, material and social circumstances. For example, low income is the strongest predictor of food insecurity in Canada, where one in eight households experiences insufficient access to nutritious foods. It's well-established that food prices are an important determinant of food choice. Low-income households report that they find it difficult to adopt dietary guidelines because food prices are a barrier to improving their diets. When researchers estimate the cost of diets people actually eat, higher-quality diets are typically more costly. While this may be so, it does not, in itself, prove that healthy diets are necessarily more expensive or cost-prohibitive. After all, not all socioeconomically disadvantaged people consume poor diets. We can easily think of a number of foods and recipes that are both inexpensive and nutritious. The internet is full of recipes for "eating well on a budget.”

paragraphs.A: A few years ago I found myself teaching a university class on evil. It was for third-year criminology students to help them contextualize theory and research within controversial current topics. It was a huge success. The debates were heated and interesting. I could see people's views change within the course of a single lecture. Over the past 13 years, as a student, lecturer and researcher, I've enjoyed discussing the science of evil with anyone willing to listen. What I like most is destroying the cliche (陈词滥调) of good and evil, and replacing them with scientific insight. We need a more informed way of discussing behavior that at first we cannot, or should not, begin to understand.
paragraphs.B: Without understanding, we risk dehumanizing others, writing off human beings simply because we don't comprehend them. We must try to understand what we have labeled evil. We tend to think evil is something that other people are. We think of ourselves as "good people", and even when we do morally wrong things, we understand the context of our decisions. With others, however, it is far easier to write them off. If their actions deviate (偏离) substantially from what we consider acceptable, we may label them evil. We need to be careful with this. Calling someone evil is often similar to saying they cannot change, and perhaps aren't even a human at all. However, when you actually go monster-hunting, and you look deeply at the people behind shocking behavior, you may be surprised.
paragraphs.C: As a child I used to love the Scooby-Doo cartoons. Arriving in their "Mystery Machine", the gang would have to find a monster who was terrorizing a neighborhood. They would run around looking for clues and at the end unmask the bad guy. It was always a normal person in a costume. There were no monsters. Like the Scooby crew, we may find ourselves hunting for an easy fix, one word for people who do bad things. But if we take a good look, the word "evil' is insufficient-there are no simple explanations for why humans do bad things: instead there are many, and they are all marvelously different.
paragraphs.D: Evil is typically referred to when there is deviance from social norms: formal deviance is the violation of laws, like theft, murder, and attacks, while informal deviance involves violations of social norms, like lying. Evil behavior is typically thought to embrace one or both forms. However, deviance can also describe a behavior that simply differs from the norm.
paragraphs.E: Perhaps this is where we can find the good side of our bad side. Deviating from the norm can make us villains （恶棍）, but it can also make us heroes. A child deviates from social pressures when they stand up for another child being bullied in school. A soldier deviates when they choose not to follow orders to kill an innocent civilian. An employee in a big tech company deviates when they expose its wrongdoings.
paragraphs.F: Creativity is also a deviation. Here, too, things are complex. Thinking creatively has given us modern medicine, technology and modern political structures, but it has also given us poison and nuclear weapons. Great benefit and great harm can come from the same human tendency.
paragraphs.G: In a research paper, Evil Genius, published in 2014, the behavioral scientists Francesca Gino and Scott Wiltermuth wanted to examine whether people who behave unethically in one task are more creative than others on a subsequent task, even after controlling for differences in baseline creative skills. The unethical behavior they chose was dishonesty.
paragraphs.H: Over five experiments researchers gave participants tasks in which they could cheat. In one study, they were given matrixes (矩阵) and had to find two numbers that added up to 10. Participants were asked to self-report how well they did at the end of the study: 59% cheated by saying that they solved more matrixes than they actually had. D) After each task, the researchers measured participants' performance on the Remote Associates Test. This shows participants three words at a time that appear to be unrelated, and the person has to think of a fourth word that is associated with all of them. For example, you might get "Fox, Man, Peep", or "Dust, Cereal, Fish". In order to find the linking words ("Hole" for the first, "Bowl" for the second)you need to be creative. The more you get right, the more creative you are thought to be because you have come up with uncommon associations. J) For every one of the five studies, they found the same thing-participants who cheated in the first task did better on the creativity task. Why? Like other forms of unethical behavior, lying means breaking rules. It involves being deviant, going against the social principle that people should tell the truth. Similarly, being creative involves "thinking outside the box", deviating from expectations. They involve similar thought patterns, so stimulating one stimulates the other. Can we learn from this? Perhaps. To be more creative, we could try lying in a controlled environment. Find online logic games and cheat at them, play Scrabble (拼字游戏) with a dictionary, or write a story about something that is untrue? Such tasks can get our brains thinking flexibly, beyond our normal comfort zone. This is not a call to become a compulsive (强迫性的) liar, but a controlled liar. K) In addition to benefits for creativity, deviance can be a good thing in other ways. Even Philip Zimbardo, the author of the Stanford prison experiment, who showed how easily we can be led to behave badly, believes that the future of deviance research may lie more in understanding extreme pro-social behavior, such as heroism. Like evil, we often view heroism as only a possibility for outliers for people who are abnormal. But Zimbardo asks: "What if the capability to act heroically is also fundamentally ordinary and available to all of us?" Some say we should never meet our heroes, lest they disappoint us when we find out how normal they are. But this should be liberating, not disappointing. We are all capable of behaving like outliers. It's time for us to understand deviance, and realize its potential for good as well as for harm.

questions.script:
Summer doesn't begin for two more days, but scientists are already sounding the alarm about dangerous ice melts going on right now in Greenland.
The vast island usually locks away enough fresh water in its ice sheet, which if melted can raise global sea levels by six meters. And research shows that in recent years its ice has melted faster than ever before. This month, as temperatures in northwestern Greenland approach all-time highs, researchers are encountering unusual, surprising levels of melting ice in the region.
The most significant concern here is how early this is all happening. Greenland experiences annual ice melt and growth cycles. But this year, the melting season began in early May. That's a month earlier than normal and something that's happened only once before in the historical record in 2016.
That means that not only is the ice melting very fast, it has more time to melt this summer than it would in a normal climate system. Longer melt seasons like this one seem to lead to much greater contributions to sea-level rise than in previous decades.

questions.script:
Bundles containing thousands of pounds in cash keep turning up on the streets of Blackhall Colliery in northern England, according to police. Residents of the village have been coming across bundles of £20 notes—usually worth £2,000—in the former mining village in County Durham.
The latest discovery was on Monday, meaning four of these cash bundles have been handed in this year and 13 since 2014.
The bundles are usually left in plain sight and have been scattered across the small coastal village. The owner has two weeks to collect the cash, which is then returned to the finder if not claimed, according to Peterlee Police.
A Durham Police spokesperson said the money has been returned to the lucky finders in all cases except yesterday.
Policeman John Forster said in a statement: "The circumstances remain a mystery so we would welcome any information that will help us get to the bottom of these random incidents."
He told The Northern Echo: "It isn't an affluent part of the world, so for them to find cash of that amount and instantly think about taking it to the police stations shows the community spirit there is."

questions.script:
W: It's your birthday next week. What have you got planned?
M: I'm not sure. I often feel strange on my birthday. It's like my brain decides to have a crisis.
W: It's not entirely unusual to feel anxious or sad around your birthday. Birthdays can tap into a lot of things people worry about, including their achievements in life in the past decade, or their accomplishments of the past year. Many begin to search for the meaning of their existence, leading to behaviors such as ending or starting a relationship, or plans, like starting a vigorous diet or fitness program.
M: I have wonderful friends and I love celebrating their birthdays. But I don't like being the center of attention, receiving gifts and having a fuss made. It seems to trigger a type of social anxiety. I think social media too can intensify things as birthdays now play out more publicly. Birthday reminders can be helpful, but I kind of worry I won't be able to drum up my own day and show it to look as exciting as it is supposed to be.
W: Well, to deal with the birthday blues, you should not isolate yourself. It's best to gradually face your birthday with people you trust. That would help you learn self-acceptance, or that it's okay to be the focus.
M: Perhaps. Or I could perceive my birthday as an opportunity to do something for others like asking people to make a donation instead of buying a gift.
W: Exactly. Or even simply see your birthday as an opportunity to bring people together for them to have fun.

questions.script:
Steve Miller began his career in IT back in the late 1980s. Being a deaf person in tech required a huge amount of effort in organization. Because there was no email or text message service, everything had to be done face to face, or by telephone. Communicating in meetings was very difficult. He needed a sign language interpreter for every meeting, but it was a huge effort to coordinate.
These days, although challenges still remain, it's a good time to be a deaf person in tech, says Miller. Big advances in speech recognition technology have enabled communication tools to turn live speech into text in real time on your smartphone or laptop, and sign language into text as well.
New Tech coupled with improvements in hearing aid technology and medical advances means that Miller is able to focus far more on his work. He has benefited to a great extent from a tiny hearing device in his ear. It gives him a degree of hearing, and he can use a variety of communication methods depending on the situation. He can employ lip-reading and have meetings via video instead of on the phone. These things have made a huge difference. He no longer has to worry about whether or not he can understand. He can just concentrate on how interesting the meeting might be and what he needs to get out of it in order to progress.

Don't go for a colour because it's in fashion, or you've seen it in a magazine.

options.A: Children must read at least 3 times a week.

questions.script:
Parents often hear that reading to their children is critical for supporting development, and the message is getting through to them. In fact, in the United States, a little over half of children between the ages of three and five were read to every day in 2007, and 83% of children in that age group in the same country were read to three or more times per week in 2012.
This is good news, because reading to young children helps their language and brain development. In fact, recent research has found that both the quality and quantity of shared book reading in infancy predicted later childhood vocabulary and reading skills. In other words, the more time parents spend reading, the greater the developmental benefits in their four-year-old children.
This is an important finding. But does it matter what books parents read? A new study has investigated this question. It followed infants across the second six months of life and found that when parents showed babies books that had faces or objects with specific labels, they learned more. This is in contrast to books that did not name images, or books that had the same label under each image. Books that named different characters also promoted greater learning. So what does this mean for parents? Not all books are created equal, so parents need to choose the books they share with their children with great care.

It followed infants across the second six months of life and found that when parents showed babies books that had faces or objects with specific labels, they learned more. This is in contrast to books that did not name images, or books that had the same label under each image. Books that named different characters also promoted greater learning. So what does this mean for parents? Not all books are created equal, so parents need to choose the books they share with their children with great care.
questions.expl: Choose carefully what to read to their children. 详解：事实细节题。短文最后提到“Not all books are created equal, so parents need to choose the books they share with their children with great care.”，即并非所有书都一样，父母需要谨慎选择与孩子分享的书。选项B与原文建议一致，故答案为B。 涉及知识点：听力中总结性建议（need to choose...with great care）的定位、同义替换（choose carefully 与 choose...with great care）。

questions.stem: 第 26 空
questions.expl: 详解： 【考点】副词辨析题。【语法判断】空格所在分句结构完整，不缺成分。空格前为动词短语 using the internet 与副词 almost，因此本空应填入副词。【语义判断】句意：...近一半的人表示“几乎____”使用互联网。由句意可知，本句说明美国青少年使用网络的频率，应填入程度副词，表示“持续不断地”，故答案为 D) constantly。

questions.stem: 第 27 空
questions.expl: usage 详解： 【考点】名词辨析题。【语法判断】空格处为句子主语，应填入名词。【语义判断】句意：连续____不应被误认为是无尽的享受。本句是对上一句“许多青少年对花在手机上的大部分时间并不满意”的进一步阐述，因此本空指的是“使用手机”，应填入含有“使用”意义的名词，故答案为 N) usage。

questions.stem: 第 28 空
questions.expl: 详解： 【考点】副词辨析题。【语法判断】本句不缺主语和谓语，且空格前后都是形容词，因此本空应填入副词。【语义判断】句意：佩尤研究中心关于“屏幕使用时间与设备干扰”的一项新的____代表性调查表明……。本空应填入表达某个级别的副词，以限定 representative 的范围，表示“全国性的”，故答案为 H) nationally。

questions.stem: 第 29 空
questions.expl: 详解： 【考点】形容词辨析题。【语法判断】空格前有系动词 are 和副词 worryingly，后有介词 from，应填入形容词作表语。【语义判断】句意：...不仅父母担忧青少年与手机____，许多青少年自己也是如此。下一句提到青少年花太多时间在手机上。因此本空应填入能够说明青少年与手机密不可分的关系的形容词。且需能与 from 搭配，inseparable from 意为“与...分不开的”，故答案为 G) inseparable。

questions.stem: 第 30 空
questions.expl: absorbed 详解： 【考点】动词/形容词辨析题。【语法判断】空格处与介词短语 in their phones 为后置定语，修饰 time。spend time (in) doing sth.，但备选项无动词-ing形式，故本空应填入形容词或过去分词。【语义判断】句意：...54%的人说他们花太多时间____于手机。结合上下文，本空应填入能表达“耗费，耗去(大量时间)”意思的词。absorbed 有“消耗，花去(时间)”之意，且 be absorbed in 为固定搭配，故答案为 A) absorbed。

questions.stem: 第 31 空
questions.expl: specific 详解： 【考点】形容词辨析题。【语法判断】空格前有系动词 is 和副词 hardly，应填入形容词。【语义判断】句意：她说这并不是青少年____。结合下一句“他们面临着和成年人一样的挑战”可知，这并不是青少年所“特有的”，故答案为 L) specific。

questions.stem: 第 32 空
questions.expl: context 详解： 【考点】名词辨析题。【语法判断】空格前是定冠词the，后是介词of，应填入名词。【语义判断】句意：只要他们生活在科技环境的____中，即旨在...的环境中。科技环境是青少年生活的大“背景”或“环境”，故答案为 E) context。

questions.stem: 第 33 空
questions.expl: shape 详解： 【考点】动词辨析题。【语法判断】空格前有情态动词 can，应填入动词原形。【语义判断】句意：父母与科技互动的方式可以____他们与孩子互动的方式。将备选动词代入，shape“影响，形成”符合句意，故答案为 J) shape。

questions.stem: 第 34 空
questions.expl: behavior 详解： 【考点】名词辨析题。【语法判断】空格前有动词 model 和形容词 good，应填入名词。【语义判断】句意：...父母应该树立良好的____榜样。下一句提到吃饭时收起手机等良好“行为”，故答案为 C) behavior。

questions.stem: 第 35 空
questions.expl:
exercise 详解： 【考点】动词辨析题。【语法判断】空格前有情态动词 can，应填入动词原形。【语义判断】句意：...他们可以对他们的设备____更多的控制。备选动词原形只有
F）exercise。 Section B (段落匹配) 题目出处： 文章标题为“Evil Genius”。 答案解析：

questions.stem: 36. A behavior that does not conform to social norms may be described as being deviant.
questions.expl: 【定位】D) 段最后一句：However, deviance can also describe a behavior that simply differs from the norm. (然而，反常也可以描述一种只是与正常不同的行为。) 【精析】题干中 A behavior that does not conform to social norms 对应定位句中的 a behavior that simply differs from the norm；be described as 对应 describe；being deviant 对应 deviance。题干是对定位句的同义转述。

questions.stem: 37. Various experiments found that
questions.expl: 【定位】J) 段第一句：For every one of the five studies, they found the same thing—participants who cheated in the first task did better on the creativity task. (对于五项研究中的每一项，他们都发现了同样的事情——在第一项任务中作弊的参与者在创造性任务中表现得更好。) 【精析】题干中 Various experiments 对应定位句中的 every one of the five studies；participants who cheated in the initial task performed better in the creativity test 对应 participants who cheated in the first task did better on the creativity task。题干是对定位句的同义转述。

questions.stem: 38. People may be simply considered evil if their behaviors are morally unacceptable to us.
questions.expl: 【定位】B) 段第六句：If their actions deviate substantially from what we consider acceptable, we may label them evil. (如果别人的行为严重偏离我们认为可以接受的范围，我们可能会给他们贴上邪恶的标签。) 【精析】题干中 People may be simply considered evil 对应定位句中的 we may label them evil；their behaviors are morally unacceptable to us 对应 their actions deviate substantially from what we consider acceptable。题干是对定位句的同义转述。

questions.stem: 39. The research published by two scientists was intended to examine the relationship between dishonesty and creativity.
questions.expl: 【定位】G) 段：In a research paper, Evil Genius, published in 2014, the behavioral scientists Francesca Gino and Scott Wiltermuth wanted to examine whether people who behave unethically in one task are more creative than others on a subsequent task... The unethical behavior they chose was dishonesty. (在2014年发表的一篇名为《邪恶天才》的研究论文中，行为科学家弗朗西斯卡·吉诺和斯科特·威尔特穆斯想要研究...他们选择的不道德行为是不诚实。) 【精析】题干 The research published by two scientists 对应定位段中的 a research paper... the behavioral scientists Francesca Gino and Scott Wiltermuth；intended to examine the relationship between dishonesty and creativity 是对定位段研究目的和内容的概括。题干是对定位段的归纳。

questions.stem: 40. The author's lectures sparked lively discussions in his class.
questions.expl: 【定位】A) 段第一至四句：A few years ago I found myself teaching a university class on evil... It was a huge success. The debates were heated and interesting. (几年前，“我”在大学里教一门关于邪恶的课程...这是一个巨大的成功。辩论激烈而有趣。) 【精析】题干中 The author‘s lectures 对应 teaching a university class；sparked lively discussions 对应 The debates were heated and interesting。题干是对定位句的概括。

questions.stem: 41. The researchers tested the
questions.expl: 【定位】I) 段：After each task, the researchers measured participants' performance on the Remote Associates Test. This shows participants three words at a time... and the person has to think of a fourth word that is associated with all of them. The more you get right, the more creative you are thought to be... (在完成每项任务后，研究人员测量了参与者在远程关联测试中的表现。这个测试是...参与者必须想出与所有单词相关的第4个单词。你答对的越多，人们就认为你越有创造力...) 【精析】题干中 tested the participants’ creativity 对应 measured participants‘ performance 及 the more creative you are thought to be；play a word game 对应定位段对远程关联测试（一种词汇联想游戏）的描述。题干是对定位段的概括。

questions.stem: 42. It is time we realized that deviance may be capable of doing both good and harm to individuals and society.
questions.expl: 【定位】K) 段最后一句：It‘s time for us to understand deviance, and realize its potential for good as well as for harm. (现在是我们理解反常的时候了，我们应该认识到反常既可能带来好处，也可能带来坏。) 【精析】题干中 It is time we realized 对应 It‘s time for us to understand... and realize；deviance 原文复现；both good and harm 对应 its potential for good as well as for harm。题干是对定位句的同义转述。

questions.stem: 43. The reasons for people's evil behaviors can be explained in more ways than one.
questions.expl: 【定位】C) 段最后一句：... there are no simple explanations for why humans do bad things: instead there are many, and they are all marvelously different. (人类为什么做坏事并没有简单的解释：相反，有很多，而且都惊人地不同。) 【精析】题干中 The reasons for people’s evil behaviors 对应 explanations for why humans do bad things；can be explained in more ways than one 对应 there are many, and they are all marvelously different。题干是对定位句的同义转述。

questions.stem: 44. The math task in one experiment was designed to test
questions.expl: 【定位】H) 段第一、二句：Over five experiments researchers gave participants tasks in which they could cheat. In one study, they were given matrixes and had to find two numbers that added up to 10. (在5个实验中，研究人员给参加者布置了任务，在任务中他们可以作弊。在一项研究中，他们得到了矩阵，并必须从中找到两个加起来等于10的数字。) 【精析】题干中 The math task in one experiment 对应 In one study, they were given matrixes... and had to find two numbers that added up to 10；designed to test participants‘ tendency to cheat 对应 gave participants tasks in which they could cheat。题干是对定位句的概括。

questions.stem: 45. Some creative ideas have turned out to do harm to human society.
questions.expl: 【定位】F) 段第三句：Thinking creatively has given us modern medicine, technology and modern political structures, but it has also given us poison and nuclear weapons. (创造性思维...但也给了我们毒药和核武器。) 【精析】题干中 Some creative ideas 对应 Thinking creatively；have turned out to do harm to human society 对应 has also given us poison and nuclear weapons。题干是对定位句后一部分的同义转述。 Section C (仔细阅读) Passage One 题目出处： 文章选自2016年8月16日网站文章“This Doctor Broke the Law to Engineer a Better Nursing Home, and the Death Rate Plummeted”。 答案解析：

questions.stem: 46. What has Bill Thomas been doing for a quarter of a century?

options.A: Transforming people's lifestyle.
options.B: Honoring his Harvard education.
options.C: Changing people's philosophy of life.
options.D: Shifting people's perspective on aging.

questions.expl:
详解： 【推理判断题】第一段概括其主要成就：改变老年人的游戏（changing the game for seniors）。第五段末句指出他鼓励老年人把年龄看作是生命中的一个丰富多彩的新阶段。第八段末句指出他的书指导我们如何改变对衰老和成长的看法。综合可知，托马斯一直在努力改变人们对衰老的看法，故D项正确。 【避错】
A）“改变人们的生活方式”、
B）“纪念他的哈佛教育”仅在第二段提及教育背景，并非他二十五年来所做的事。
C）“改变人们的人生哲学”文中未涉及；

questions.stem: 47. Why did Bill Thomas try something different in the nursing home?

options.A: He wanted to make it more pleasant for seniors.
options.B: He wanted to apply his Harvard training to practice.
options.C: He felt it his duty to revolutionize its management.
options.D: He felt disappointed working in the environment.

questions.expl:
He wanted to make it more pleasant for seniors. 详解： 【推理判断题】第二段末句提到，压抑而严格管制的环境让他思考如何改善老年人的生活条件（improve the residents‘ conditions）。第四段指出，在他采取措施后，老人们更快乐了（the residents were simply happier）。由此可见，其目的是为了让养老院对老人来说更愉快，故A项正确。 【避错】
B）“将哈佛训练应用于实践”、
C）“改革其管理体制”文中未提及；
D）“对工作环境感到失望”是对“depressing and regimented environment”的过度推断，原文客观描述环境，并未表达他的个人情绪。

questions.stem: 48. What do we learn about Bill Thomas bringing animals and plants into the nursing home?

options.A: He made a mess of the nursing home.
options.B: He did something all professionals would do.
options.C: He won instant support from the state authorities.
options.D: He acted in violation of the state law.

questions.expl:
He acted in violation of the state law. 详解： 【细节辨认题】第三段第一句明确指出：尽管当时在养老院饲养动物是违法的（animals in nursing homes were illegal），比尔·托马斯医生还是冒险一试。故D项正确。 【避错】
A）“他把养老院弄得一团糟”与第四段描述的积极变化相反；
B）“他做了所有专业人士都会做的事”无依据；
C）“他立即获得了州当局的支持”文中未提及。

questions.stem: 49. What has Bill Thomas been persistently advocating?

options.A: Good health is not just a privilege of the young.
options.B: Nursing homes should be strictly limited in size.
options.C: Getting old is by no means something miserable.
options.D: Residences for seniors should be run independently.

questions.expl:
Getting old is by no means something miserable. 详解： 【细节辨认题】第六段末句指出：他一直在宣扬一个特别的信息——变老并不是一件坏事（getting old is not a bad thing）。故C项正确。 【避错】
A）“身体健康不仅仅是年轻人的特权”未提及；
B）“养老院的规模应受到严格限制”是对第七段“建筑太大”评论的曲解；
D）“老年人住所应独立运营”是其具体做法之一，并非他一直宣扬的核心信息。

questions.stem: 50. How is Bill Thomas's new concept received?

options.A: It is gaining ground in many countries.
options.B: It is being heatedly debated worldwide.
options.C: It is considered revolutionary everywhere.
options.D: It is winning approval from the government.

questions.expl:
It is gaining ground in many countries. 详解： 【推理判断题】倒数第二段第一句指出：托马斯的方法已经被澳大利亚、日本、加拿大和美国采用，并取得了巨大的成功（adopted... with enormous success）。由此可知，他的新观念正在许多国家获得认可和推广，故A项正确。 【避错】
B）“正在全世界被热烈讨论”、
C）“被认为是革命性的”文中未明确提及；
D）“赢得了政府的认可”文中未提及政府态度。 Passage Two 题目出处： 文章选自2018年10月8日《对话》杂志官网文章“Time and money—the biggest hurdles to healthy eating”。 答案解析：

questions.stem: 51. What can we learn from research on diets in developed countries?

options.A: Dietary recommendations are not fit for underprivileged people.
options.B: People from different social groups vary in their dietary habits.
options.C: People's choice of food depends on their individual taste.
options.D: There is no consensus on what high-quality diets are.

questions.expl:
People from different social groups vary in their dietary habits. 详解： 【推理判断题】首段第一、二句指出：研究表明，更富裕和受教育程度更高的人倾向于消费更高质量的饮食；相反，经济困难的人饮食低营养、高能量。由此可见，不同社会群体的人饮食习惯不相同，故B项正确。 【避错】
A）“膳食建议不适合贫困人群”是过度推断，首段只说他们不太可能符合建议；
C）“人们对食物的选择取决于个人口味”、
D）“对高质量饮食没有共识”文中未提及。

questions.stem: 52. What does the author say is important in formulating policies to improve diets and health?

options.A: A better understanding of the relationship between social class and health.
options.B: A greater emphasis on studying the cause of obesity and chronic diseases.
options.C: Prioritizing the provision of better nutrition for lower classes.
options.D: Designing education programs and initiatives on public health.

questions.expl:
详解： 【细节辨认题】第二段第二、三句提到：社会阶层与饮食质量和健康之间的关系有充分文献证明；然而，研究并未解释为什么会出现这种情况——这个问题对于设计有效的政策和计划具有重要意义。因此，更好地理解这种关系很重要，故A项正确。 【避错】
B）“更重视研究肥胖和慢性病的原因”是对第二段第一句的曲解，该句描述现象而非强调研究原因；
C）“优先为下层阶级提供更好营养”未提及；
D）“设计公共健康教育项目和计划”是第三段提到的现有做法，并非题干所问“制定政策时重要的”内容。

questions.stem: 53. What does research reveal about adults in food-insecure households?

options.A: Their eating habits need to be changed.
options.B: Their food literacy has been improving.
options.C: They do not pay much attention to their food recipes.
options.D: They do not lack food knowledge or budgeting skills.

questions.expl:
They do not lack food knowledge or budgeting skills. 详解： 【细节辨认题】第四段第一、二句指出：研究表明，生活在食物不足家庭的成年人，和生活在食物充足家庭的成年人一样，有可能调整食谱使其更健康，也同样精通食物准备和烹饪技巧。这说明他们并不缺乏食物知识或技能，故D项正确。 【避错】
A）“他们的饮食习惯需要改变”、
B）“他们的食物知识水平一直在提高”文中未提及趋势。
C）“他们不太关注食物食谱”均与第四段研究结论相反；

questions.stem: 54. What would help improve food security among the disadvantaged groups in Canada?

options.A: Teaching them budgeting skills.
options.B: Increasing their food choices.
options.C: Enabling them to have more access to nutritious foods.
options.D: Taking more effective measures to increase food supplies.

questions.expl:
详解： 【推理判断题】第五段末句以加拿大为例指出：低收入是食物不足的最强预测因素，八分之一的家庭无法获得有营养的食物（insufficient access to nutritious foods）。因此，改善弱势群体食物安全，有效措施应是使他们能更多地获得有营养的食品，故C项正确。 【避错】第四段末句明确说没有迹象表明提高预算技能会减少食物不足，故A错；
B）“增加食物选择”、
D）“采取更有效措施增加食物供应”均非第五段例子直接推导出的针对性建议。

questions.stem: 55. What does the author suggest disadvantaged people do to improve their health?

options.A: Adopt a positive attitude towards dietary guidelines.
options.B: Choose diets that are both healthy and affordable.
options.C: Make sure to purchase healthy foods on the internet.
options.D: Change their eating habits and consumption patterns.

questions.expl:
详解： 【推理判断题】最后两段指出：健康饮食不一定更贵；我们可以想到许多既便宜又有营养的食物和食谱；互联网上到处都是“省钱吃得好”的食谱。由此可推断，作者建议弱势群体选择既健康又负担得起的饮食，故B项正确。 【避错】

The World Pipe Band Championships will take place in Glasgow on Saturday.
Over 120 of the world's best pipe bands will compete at the championships. Over 4,000 pipers and drummers are expected to descend on the city for the annual event.
It will take place at the St. James Playing Fields in Glasgow on Saturday, 18 May from 10:00 am until 7:00 pm. The event is free. Also, a free shuttle bus will run between the event car parks and the competition site. Shuttle buses will run every 15 minutes from 8:00 am until 8:00 pm.
Glasgow City Council says it is estimated to bring £300,000 to the local economy.
The first World Pipe Band Championships were held in Edinburgh in 1947. The event first took place in Glasgow in 1948. It has been held regularly in Glasgow since 1986.

Summer doesn't begin for two more days, but scientists are already sounding the alarm about dangerous ice melts going on right now in Greenland.
The vast island usually locks away enough fresh water in its ice sheet, which if melted can raise global sea levels by six meters. And research shows that in recent years its ice has melted faster than ever before. This month, as temperatures in northwestern Greenland approach all-time highs, researchers are encountering unusual, surprising levels of melting ice in the region.
The most significant concern here is how early this is all happening. Greenland experiences annual ice melt and growth cycles. But this year, the melting season began in early May. That's a month earlier than normal and something that's happened only once before in the historical record in 2016.
That means that not only is the ice melting very fast, it has more time to melt this summer than it would in a normal climate system. Longer melt seasons like this one seem to lead to much greater contributions to sea-level rise than in previous decades.

Bundles containing thousands of pounds in cash keep turning up on the streets of Blackhall Colliery in northern England, according to police. Residents of the village have been coming across bundles of £20 notes—usually worth £2,000—in the former mining village in County Durham.
The latest discovery was on Monday, meaning four of these cash bundles have been handed in this year and 13 since 2014.
The bundles are usually left in plain sight and have been scattered across the small coastal village. The owner has two weeks to collect the cash, which is then returned to the finder if not claimed, according to Peterlee Police.
A Durham Police spokesperson said the money has been returned to the lucky finders in all cases except yesterday.
Policeman John Forster said in a statement: "The circumstances remain a mystery so we would welcome any information that will help us get to the bottom of these random incidents."
He told The Northern Echo: "It isn't an affluent part of the world, so for them to find cash of that amount and instantly think about taking it to the police stations shows the community spirit there is."

W: It's your birthday next week. What have you got planned?
M: I'm not sure. I often feel strange on my birthday. It's like my brain decides to have a crisis.
W: It's not entirely unusual to feel anxious or sad around your birthday. Birthdays can tap into a lot of things people worry about, including their achievements in life in the past decade, or their accomplishments of the past year. Many begin to search for the meaning of their existence, leading to behaviors such as ending or starting a relationship, or plans, like starting a vigorous diet or fitness program.
M: I have wonderful friends and I love celebrating their birthdays. But I don't like being the center of attention, receiving gifts and having a fuss made. It seems to trigger a type of social anxiety. I think social media too can intensify things as birthdays now play out more publicly. Birthday reminders can be helpful, but I kind of worry I won't be able to drum up my own day and show it to look as exciting as it is supposed to be.
W: Well, to deal with the birthday blues, you should not isolate yourself. It's best to gradually face your birthday with people you trust. That would help you learn self-acceptance, or that it's okay to be the focus.
M: Perhaps. Or I could perceive my birthday as an opportunity to do something for others like asking people to make a donation instead of buying a gift.
W: Exactly. Or even simply see your birthday as an opportunity to bring people together for them to have fun.

Steve Miller began his career in IT back in the late 1980s. Being a deaf person in tech required a huge amount of effort in organization. Because there was no email or text message service, everything had to be done face to face, or by telephone. Communicating in meetings was very difficult. He needed a sign language interpreter for every meeting, but it was a huge effort to coordinate.
These days, although challenges still remain, it's a good time to be a deaf person in tech, says Miller. Big advances in speech recognition technology have enabled communication tools to turn live speech into text in real time on your smartphone or laptop, and sign language into text as well.
New Tech coupled with improvements in hearing aid technology and medical advances means that Miller is able to focus far more on his work. He has benefited to a great extent from a tiny hearing device in his ear. It gives him a degree of hearing, and he can use a variety of communication methods depending on the situation. He can employ lip-reading and have meetings via video instead of on the phone. These things have made a huge difference. He no longer has to worry about whether or not he can understand. He can just concentrate on how interesting the meeting might be and what he needs to get out of it in order to progress.

Colour is now spreading through our homes, up staircases, across wood frames and ceilings, filling in neutral spaces.
According to one interior designer, when people return home, they want to see colours that cheer them up and give them a hug. Pure white walls simply don't do that. They don't look after you.
Another interior designer commented that certain combinations can key into something on a deeper level, transporting you to a different moment in time. That's the power of colour.
If you are thinking to try colour on some of your neutral walls, the advice is refreshingly simple: Choose a colour you actually like.
Don't go for a colour because it's in fashion, or you've seen it in a magazine.
If you're weary of full colour, test your tolerance with smaller spaces, such as the inside of a cupboard or a bright window frame. If it gives you joy every time you open the cupboard, you can start to take it further.
One can also paint the wooden frameworks the same colour as the walls, helping the rooms look bigger. In the kitchen, painting the overhead cupboards and the walls in the same colour can make it feel more spacious.
While painting the kitchen counters, a bold colour can make everything feel more open and lighter. Additionally, a painted ceiling is a magical thing without being too obvious and can affect how the space feels as well.

Parents often hear that reading to their children is critical for supporting development, and the message is getting through to them. In fact, in the United States, a little over half of children between the ages of three and five were read to every day in 2007, and 83% of children in that age group in the same country were read to three or more times per week in 2012.
This is good news, because reading to young children helps their language and brain development. In fact, recent research has found that both the quality and quantity of shared book reading in infancy predicted later childhood vocabulary and reading skills. In other words, the more time parents spend reading, the greater the developmental benefits in their four-year-old children.
This is an important finding. But does it matter what books parents read? A new study has investigated this question. It followed infants across the second six months of life and found that when parents showed babies books that had faces or objects with specific labels, they learned more. This is in contrast to books that did not name images, or books that had the same label under each image. Books that named different characters also promoted greater learning. So what does this mean for parents? Not all books are created equal, so parents need to choose the books they share with their children with great care.
